title: Reading him honestly
hookLine: some of his views reflect his time, and later readers wrestle with them openly

lines: A PAGE THAT STOPS YOU COLD.
RIP IT, HIDE IT, OR TOSS IT?
cards: A treasured book, a beloved teacher, and then a page that stops the reader cold: a line about who can learn, or who matters, that lands badly today. There are a few easy ways out. Rip out the page.
Pretend you never saw it. Or throw away the whole book. Readers of Maimonides meet pages like that.
And the surprising thing is that Maimonides himself handed them a better way to handle it.

teach.h: ACCEPT THE TRUTH FROM WHOEVER SAYS IT.
teach.b: Reading him honestly. First, his own rule. In the introduction to his Eight Chapters, Maimonides says he drew on the words of sages and of philosophers, and that a person should accept the truth from whoever says it.
Truth isn't weighed by the name on it. Second, he did this to the sages. In the Guide he takes up the astronomy found in the Talmud, where some details don't fit what was known in his day.

teach.h: THE SAGES' ASTRONOMY WAS OF ITS TIME.
teach.b: Don't be troubled, he says: the sages' astronomy came from the science of their own time, not from prophecy. He honored them, and still said where their knowledge was of its age. Third, a page of his own.
In his laws of Torah study, Maimonides writes that a woman who studies Torah receives a reward.
Then he adds that the sages commanded a father not to teach his daughter Torah, and gives a reason about women's minds that some readers today find painful.
There are other passages too, about other peoples, that some readers wince at.
Fourth, wrestling in the open. Later readers haven't hidden these lines.
Some read them narrowly, as limited to one kind of study. Some say, as he said of the sages, that here he spoke from his own time. Some simply disagree with him.
Today girls and women study Torah in communities across the Jewish world, and they read Maimonides too.
Reading him honestly means keeping the whole page in view: the brilliance and the blind spot, side by side, with no need to tear either one out.

how: Jewish study often reads a classic text together with later commentators who question it, so disagreement with a great teacher is part of learning him, and different communities handle hard passages in different ways.

o: keeping both his brilliance and his blind spots in view
cutting out the lines that no longer fit today
defending every line a great teacher ever wrote

games.q: you love Maimonides, and you find a line of his that hurts to read. what do you do?
o: keep the whole page in view and wrestle with it.
games.why: later readers keep the page and argue with it, the way he himself said the sages' astronomy was of its time.

practice: Bring to mind an old text you care about, scripture, a family letter, a book that shaped you, and find one line in it that troubles you. Don't rush to fix it, and don't throw the rest away.
Just hold the two side by side for a few breaths: what you would keep forever, and the line you can't accept.

wordCard.voice: Reading him honestly. Accepting truth from whoever says it, and naming where a great teacher spoke from his own time, without hiding either. Today's word.
